About This Part
Volume 8F is the final Google Cloud section of the DevOps Master Course. It converts product knowledge into
senior engineering judgment. The emphasis is on architecture decisions, verified operations, measurable
reliability, secure migration, incident leadership, cost accountability, and portfolio evidence that can withstand
technical review. The work is deliberately scenario-driven. Every chapter asks you to define requirements, compare alternatives,
select a design, implement a controlled exercise, collect evidence, explain residual risk, and improve the
operating model. Completed labs should become diagrams, architecture decision records, infrastructure-as-code
repositories, runbooks, dashboards, test reports, and concise portfolio case studies. Graduation principle: a production claim is credible only when another engineer can reproduce the
evidence, observe the result, understand the trade-off, and execute the recovery procedure. Safety, Security, and Cost Controls

Chapter 56 - Architecture Decisions, Trade-offs, and Well-
Architected Reviews
Turning business goals into measurable, reviewable, evidence-backed Google Cloud decisions
Learning Objectives

Translate business outcomes into functional requirements, constraints, and quality-attribute scenarios.

Apply the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework across operational excellence, security, reliability,
performance, cost, and sustainability.

Create architecture decision records and distinguish reversible experiments from high-consequence
commitments.

Run cross-functional architecture reviews that produce prioritized actions and accepted-risk statements.
56.1 Requirements and Quality Attributes
Architecture begins with outcomes, not products. Convert statements such as “the platform must be highly
available” into a quality-attribute scenario that names the source of a stimulus, the stimulus, the environment,
the affected component, the expected response, and the response measure. A useful requirement might state
that when one serving region becomes unavailable during peak load, authenticated requests continue through
another region with no data loss beyond the agreed RPO and with recovery completed inside the RTO. Capture regulatory boundaries, latency targets, growth assumptions, data residency, identity model, release
frequency, support hours, recovery expectations, cost envelope, sustainability goals, and team capability. Unknowns become explicit assumptions with owners and validation dates rather than hidden facts.
56.2 Well-Architected Trade-offs
The Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework provides a common review language.

56.2 Well-Architected Trade-offs
The Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework provides a common review language. A design can improve one
pillar while creating pressure elsewhere: multi-region replication can improve availability but increase cost,
operational complexity, and data-consistency risk; strict data perimeters can reduce exfiltration risk but
complicate integration and support. Prioritize risks by business impact and uncertainty rather than attempting to score every recommendation
equally. Evidence should include service-level indicators, error budgets, deployment history, audit findings,
restore tests, security detections, cost reports, capacity tests, and game-day outcomes.
56.3 Architecture Decision Records
An architecture decision record captures context, decision, alternatives, consequences, status, owner, and
review trigger. ADRs preserve organizational memory and prevent teams from repeatedly reopening old
choices without new evidence. High-quality ADRs identify the decision boundary and explicitly describe what the decision does not solve. For
example, choosing Cloud Run for a stateless API does not decide the database consistency model, regional
topology, queue semantics, or customer identity architecture.
56.4 Review Process and Decision Quality
Architecture review is a risk-discovery mechanism, not a diagram approval meeting. Include application, data,
security, networking, operations, reliability, finance, compliance, and business representatives. Review
assumptions, failure modes, operational ownership, migration path, rollback, and evidence quality.

Chapter 57 - Enterprise SaaS and AI-Enabled Platform Architecture
Designing secure, tenant-aware, globally scalable software platforms on Google Cloud
Learning Objectives

Choose tenant-isolation models based on risk, scale, customization, and cost.

Design tenant-aware identity, routing, data partitioning, quotas, metering, and lifecycle automation.

Use cells, rings, feature flags, and tenant-level telemetry to limit blast radius.

Integrate generative AI or agent capabilities without weakening data isolation, privacy, or cost controls.
57.1 Tenant Isolation and Cell Architecture
SaaS isolation is a spectrum. Shared infrastructure maximizes utilization; dedicated projects, clusters,
databases, or encryption boundaries maximize isolation. Many enterprises combine models by tenant tier,
jurisdiction, workload sensitivity, and support requirements. A cell architecture groups a bounded set of tenants with independent serving, data, and operational
components. Cells reduce correlated failure and enable progressive rollout. A control plane handles tenant
placement and lifecycle, while data-plane cells continue operating during control-plane degradation.
57.2 Identity, Routing, and Data Boundaries
Tenant identity must originate from a trusted identity provider and be carried through every authorization
decision. Never accept tenant identity solely from an untrusted request field. Use tenant-aware routing at the
load balancer, API layer, or application gateway, then enforce authorization again inside the workload. Partition relational, document, analytical, vector, and object data with explicit tenant keys and verified query
patterns. High-assurance tiers may justify dedicated projects, encryption keys, databases, or regions.

and telemetry must include tenant context without leaking sensitive payloads.
57.3 Provisioning, Metering, and Lifecycle
Tenant onboarding should be idempotent: validate entitlement, select isolation tier and region, provision
through versioned automation, configure identity and secrets, create quotas and dashboards, run synthetic
tests, and emit a durable completion event. Offboarding must support suspend, export, legal hold, retention,
deletion, and evidence of completion. Metering events require stable identifiers, deduplication, reconciliation, late-event handling, and a clear
distinction between usage telemetry and financial billing records. Build cost allocation by tenant, cell,
environment, and product capability.
57.4 AI and Agent Guardrails
AI-enabled SaaS introduces prompt, retrieval, model, tool, and output boundaries. Tenant context must
constrain retrieval and tool execution. Use approved models, data-loss prevention, content controls, grounding
evaluation, prompt-injection defenses, tool allowlists, and human approval for high-impact actions. Measure token or inference cost, latency, quality, safety, and tenant-level limits. Treat model versions and
prompts as deployable artifacts with evaluation evidence and rollback. Never assume a managed AI service
automatically supplies application-level authorization. SaaS principle: tenant context is a security boundary, an operational dimension, a cost dimension, and
a recovery dimension - not merely a database column.

Chapter 58 - Hybrid Cloud, Distributed Cloud, and Migration
Factories
Assessing estates, building foundations, and moving workloads through repeatable migration waves
Learning Objectives

Rationalize workloads using retire, retain, rehost, replatform, refactor, repurchase, and relocate decisions.

Use discovery evidence and dependency mapping to create migration waves.

Design hybrid identity, networking, operations, data, and security boundaries.

Build a migration factory with repeatable intake, landing, validation, cutover, rollback, and optimization.
58.1 Strategy and Workload Rationalization
Migration is a portfolio transformation, not a sequence of copy operations. Define business drivers, deadlines,
exit costs, regulatory obligations, modernization appetite, operating-model readiness, and success measures
before selecting tooling. Rationalization decisions must reflect technical fit and business value. A low-value unsupported application
may be retired; a stable vendor product may be repurchased as SaaS; a tightly coupled estate may first be
rehosted to meet a data-center exit and modernized later.
58.2 Discovery, Dependencies, and Wave Planning
Use inventory, utilization, application ownership, network flows, authentication, DNS, data movement, batch
schedules, licenses, certificates, and support dependencies. Dependency confidence matters: unknown
dependencies should increase wave risk and require additional observation. Create waves around dependency groups and business calendars.

58.3 Hybrid and Distributed Operations
Hybrid architecture spans identity federation, Cloud Interconnect or HA VPN, routing, DNS, certificate trust,
logging, monitoring, patching, backup, configuration, and incident escalation. Treat the connection and
management plane as products with SLOs and tested failover. Google Distributed Cloud or other edge and hybrid platforms can extend consistent operations where latency,
data sovereignty, disconnected operation, or local processing requires it. The operating model must clearly
separate Google-managed, customer-managed, and shared responsibilities.
58.4 Migration Factory Operating Model
A migration factory standardizes intake, assessment, landing-zone readiness, application remediation, data
synchronization, rehearsal, cutover, validation, and optimization. Standardization should reduce avoidable
variance while preserving an exception path for unusual workloads. Measure lead time, wave success, rollback frequency, defect escape, dependency surprises, post-cutover
incidents, cost variance, and optimization backlog. A migration is not complete until operations, security,
backup, cost ownership, and support have accepted the workload. Migration principle: move evidence, ownership, and recovery capability with the workload - not only
compute and data. Production Design Checklist

Chapter 59 - Application Modernization and Monolith
Decomposition
Moving from tightly coupled systems to independently deployable, observable, resilient capabilities
Learning Objectives

Select modernization approaches based on business value, coupling, risk, and team capability.

Use decomposition patterns such as strangler, branch by abstraction, event interception, and modular
monolith.

Manage data ownership, distributed transactions, compatibility, and migration sequencing.

Choose GKE, Cloud Run, managed services, or retained VMs based on workload characteristics.
59.1 Modernization Decision Framework
Modernization is justified when it changes business velocity, reliability, security, scalability, cost, or
maintainability enough to repay transformation risk. Avoid decomposing merely to adopt fashionable products. Assess domain boundaries, release coupling, change failure rate, testability, operational maturity, data
ownership, latency sensitivity, compliance, and team structure. A modular monolith can be a better
intermediate state than prematurely distributed microservices.
59.2 Decomposition Patterns
The strangler pattern routes selected capabilities to new implementations while the monolith continues serving
the remainder. Branch by abstraction changes internal interfaces before moving implementations. Event
interception captures useful domain events without rewriting the entire transaction path. Use anti-corruption layers when new domain models must interact with legacy data or protocols. Define
retirement criteria for old paths; otherwise the organization accumulates permanent dual systems.
59.3 Data Ownership and Consistency
Data decomposition is usually harder than compute decomposition.

59.3 Data Ownership and Consistency
Data decomposition is usually harder than compute decomposition. Establish authoritative ownership,
migration states, reconciliation, idempotency, schema compatibility, and fallback. Avoid shared-database
coupling that allows every service to update every table. Use sagas, outbox patterns, change data capture, and compensating actions where atomic cross-service
transactions are not possible. Explicitly choose consistency and failure behavior instead of inheriting it
accidentally.
59.4 Platform and Operating Model
Cloud Run is appropriate for many stateless HTTP, event, job, and worker workloads; GKE provides deeper
Kubernetes control and a broad platform surface; Compute Engine remains valid for specialized or legacy
requirements. Managed databases, Pub/Sub, Eventarc, Workflows, and API products can remove
undifferentiated operations. Modernization also requires service ownership, on-call readiness, SLOs, dependency maps, secure delivery,
telemetry, cost allocation, and incident response. More services without stronger operations create more failure
modes, not more agility. Modernization principle: decompose around business capability and ownership, not around technical
layers or arbitrary repository boundaries. Production Design Checklist




Compatibility and rollback exist during coexistence.

Each new service has SLO, owner, runbook, and cost allocation.

Legacy paths have retirement dates. Troubleshooting Matrix

Chapter 60 - Multi-Region and Global Application Design
Designing global ingress, data, dependency, failover, and recovery behavior
Learning Objectives

Compare active-passive, active-active, and cell-based regional topologies.

Design global ingress and dependency locality with Google Cloud load balancing and DNS.

Choose data replication and consistency models aligned to RTO, RPO, and user experience.

Create deterministic failover, failback, and recovery orchestration.
60.1 Global Topologies
Active-passive topologies concentrate writes in one region and maintain a warm or cold recovery region. They
can simplify consistency but require tested activation. Active-active topologies serve multiple regions
simultaneously and can improve latency and availability, but introduce routing, data, conflict, and operational
complexity. Cell-based topologies bound tenant or customer groups to independent regional cells. Global systems often
combine patterns: global stateless ingress, regional cells, and a separately governed global control plane.
60.2 Ingress and Dependency Locality
Global external load balancing can route users to healthy backends, but application availability still depends on

63.1 Workload Model and Performance Budget
Performance engineering begins with traffic shape: request mix, payload size, concurrency, geographic
distribution, read/write ratio, cache hit rate, batch windows, queue behavior, and growth. Average load hides
peaks and correlations. Define budgets for end-to-end latency, server time, dependency time, queue delay, error rate, throughput,
saturation, and cost per transaction. Include percentile targets rather than only averages.
63.2 Test Types and Environments

load test proves expected demand; a stress test discovers failure boundaries; a soak test finds leaks and slow
degradation; a failover test measures recovery under load. Representative tests require realistic data distribution, authentication, caching, network path, dependency
behavior, and autoscaling settings. Protect shared environments and define stop conditions.
63.3 Bottleneck Analysis
Correlate user latency with application traces, CPU throttling, memory pressure, garbage collection, connection
pools, storage latency, database locks, query plans, cache behavior, queue age, network loss, and downstream
saturation. Avoid tuning one metric in isolation.

63.4 Capacity, Autoscaling, and Quotas
